findings.title: Findings converge on D2's retire-at-stop reconcile call
findings.why_it_matters: Decision D2 (what a config change that adds or removes an instance restarts) retires a removed instance's rows by calling `reconcile_app_registrations(app_key, {}, instance_name=name)` at the stop. That function was built for a different job: after an instance is ready, it compares rows against the instance's live ids. Four findings land on this one call from different angles. It can delete a row whose execution is still queued (Finding 2). It sits inside the stop phase with every app-key lock held (Finding 3). Its once=True branch can raise and roll the whole call back (Finding 4). Its input comes from a config diff, not from what is tracked (Finding 5). Each finding proposes its own local fix, and three of those fixes add a rule to this call. The question for you: does this point to a problem with the call itself that should be re-evaluated, rather than patched finding by finding? Re-evaluation is open-ended: it includes whether the call is needed at all, and whether these failure modes are limitations to accept and document.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate D2's at-stop reconcile call before addressing the converging findings individually. Open questions: Is an at-stop retire worth having at all, given the sweep retires removed rows within one retention cycle? Which operation should do the retiring? When should it run relative to the stop phase, the create phase, and lock release? Should a stop that left work running have its rows retired? What defines "removed": the config diff or the registry?
findings.choice_reason: Re-evaluation settled on enqueuing the sweep retire step after the stop half

findings.title: D2's reconcile deletes rows that a queued or still-running execution points at
findings.why_it_matters: With empty live sets, the reconcile deletes every non-once listener and job row of that instance that has no execution row yet, and retires the rest. Execution records are enqueued fire-and-forget and flushed in batches, up to `max_flush_interval_seconds` later (default 5s), while the reconcile goes through `submit`. So the delete can run first. The foreign key question is settled: it is enforced. `database_service.py:550` sets `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`, and `executions.listener_id` and `job_id` reference their parents. A late insert fails on the foreign key. The fallback nulls the key and retries, the retry fails the table's "exactly one of listener_id, job_id" CHECK, and the row is dropped. The loss is that one execution, plus the batch's completion events, with an ERROR log and a `dropped_exhausted` count. The other rows in the batch survive. A probe against the fully migrated schema reproduced this sequence. The loss is bounded and logged, so this stays MEDIUM. A stop that hung or raised is the same case without the time window: the leftover work's executions keep getting dropped. The ledger doesn't say the call is skipped for a flagged stop.
findings.recommended: B: Retire removed names' rows at the reload, with no delete.

findings.title: D2's reconcile call waits on the database during the all-locks stop phase
findings.why_it_matters: The call runs while every affected app-key lock is held and before any create starts, so a database stall delays the whole reload. The critic called this an unbounded await on a path the reload never needed. The code is narrower than that. `wait_for_ready` is bounded by `startup_timeout_seconds` (10s prod, 20s dev), and `submit` is bounded until the write starts by `write_submit_timeout_seconds`; its `TimeoutError` is caught and logged as a warning. Only a write that has started and then wedges is unbounded. The create path already awaits this same call under the same locks (`app_lifecycle_instances.py:103`). What's new is smaller: a removal-only edit now touches the database, and a stall delays creates by up to those bounds per removed name.
findings.recommended: C: Accept as a known limitation: a database stall during a removal delays that reload by up to the existing timeouts, the same exposure the create path has.

findings.title: D2's once=True branch can roll back the whole retire, and the ledger doesn't state once=True behavior
findings.why_it_matters: The critic said a removed instance's once=True rows with older-session history get hard-deleted, routinely. Checking the code changes this in two ways. First, those rows normally don't exist by then: `_do_cleanup_once_listeners` removes them, and their executions, at every session start. Unfired once rows have no history and delete cleanly, and rows fired this session keep `removed_at`, so they are not in the active views. D2's "gone at the reload" holds for the normal cases. Second, if such a row does survive, the delete doesn't succeed: `ON DELETE SET NULL` violates the exactly-one CHECK, the transaction raises and rolls back, and the removed instance's non-once rows aren't retired either. The result is a WARNING, then the sweep retires them within one retention cycle. This was run through the real `TelemetryRepository.reconcile_registrations` against a fully migrated database. `session_manager.py:153-157` documents the same constraint for its own delete. The SQL is unchanged from `origin/main`, so the failure exists on the default branch for any non-live once row that survives cleanup. D2 adds one more way to reach it.
findings.recommended: C: Accept as a known limitation: if startup once-listener cleanup failed, a removal's retire rolls back with a warning and the sweep retires the rows within one retention cycle.

findings.title: D2's removed set comes from a config diff, not from what is tracked
findings.why_it_matters: `_plan_reload` diffs the old config against the new one, so "removed" means "in the old config, not in the new one". An instance tracked in the registry but absent from the old config baseline, such as one left over from an earlier partly failed reload, is in neither set, so it gets no stop and no retire. Today a count change takes the full-reload branch, which stops every tracked target through `_stop_targets`. D2 deletes that branch, so this catch-all goes away. The fallback is the sweep, whose `live_instances()` reads config plus running instances, so the row outcome is stale handler rows and not corruption.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: an instance tracked outside the config diff isn't stopped by a later edit, and stays until a full reload or restart, with its rows retired by the sweep.

findings.title: The ledger doesn't say what replaces the under-lock index check, or that a route translates once
findings.why_it_matters: `_instance_index_in_range` re-checks after the app-key lock because config can change while a caller waits. The Summary says nothing below the route layer takes an index, but never says what the check becomes. A Build could let it degrade to "name not tracked", and then `start_instance` could create an instance for a name the config just removed. The index-to-name read also appears in three places in a request (`_require_valid_instance_index`, `_orphan_instance_permitted`, the route). They can't diverge while they run without an await between them, but only if the route translates once and passes the name down.
findings.chosen: Add to the Summary's "Index-to-name lookup" bullet: "Each instance route translates index to name once and passes the name down. `_instance_index_in_range` becomes a check that the name is in the manifest's configured names, re-checked under the app-key lock as today. `stop_instance` keeps skipping it, so an orphan stays stoppable." The senior-engineer critic's related suggestion, echoing the index at response time in `ActionResponse`, is left out: it changes a response for a field #3100 removes in the same release.

findings.title: Prune and in-config rules are defined by index arithmetic, and the ledger doesn't restate them by name
findings.why_it_matters: `prune_stale_failed_indices` removes non-running entries with `index >= count`, and `_index_in_current_config` is `index < len(configs)`. Neither has a meaning under names, and the Summary lists the methods without a rule. The Build also has to settle a few smaller points the ledger leaves open: `AppRestart.indices` becoming names, `_target_names` for a name present on only one side, and when `ActionOutcomes` reads the display index across a reload's stop and create halves.
findings.chosen: Add to the Summary's "Instance and needs-restart maps" bullet: "`prune_stale_failed_indices` removes non-running entries whose name isn't configured, and keeps needs-restart records as today. `_index_in_current_config` becomes the same membership test. A class-load failure records against the first configured name that is neither running nor flagged." Add to the "Selective restart" bullet: "`AppRestart.indices` becomes names." Leave `ActionOutcomes` display-index timing and `_target_names` for one-sided names to the Build, recorded under "Calls made during the build".

findings.title: D5 needs resolve_cache_keys to read resolved names, and two docstrings still describe the index
findings.why_it_matters: `resolve_cache_keys` builds keys from `len(manifest.app_config)` and the docstrings of `resolve_cache_keys` and `unsafe_app_key_reason` describe `{app_key}/{index}`, as does a comment in `unsafe_cache_path_reason`. D5 names `resolve_cache_keys` but not how it gets names or the stale text. Names are safe to read there: `AppManifest` validation resolves them before `warn_on_cache_key_collisions` runs. The instance-name charset also rules out traversal and clashes with the old digit directories. The critic's concern that the collision warning's default-key path goes dead isn't a change from today: two different apps' default keys can't collide now either, because an app key is one path segment. Upgrade effects (empty caches, orphaned directories) are ratified in D5 and aren't raised again.
findings.chosen: Add to D5's Situation: "`resolve_cache_keys` takes each name from `normalize_app_config(manifest.app_config)`, already resolved by manifest validation. The docstrings of `resolve_cache_keys` and `unsafe_app_key_reason`, and the comment in `unsafe_cache_path_reason`, move to `{app_key}/{instance_name}`."

findings.title: A moved name can register in the same owner namespace as a flagged teardown's leftovers
findings.why_it_matters: `owner_id` is the instance name. A flagged instance has a task that may still call `self.bus.on` or `scheduler.run_*`. If its name moves to another app before Hassette restarts, those registrations land in the new instance's namespace, and a late teardown can remove the new instance's registrations. D6 (what a needs-restart flag does on a rename or move) ratified accepting this, so it's raised once against that stance. D6 relies on the old name staying visibly FAILED. For a moved name there is no separate signal at creation that an overlap exists.
findings.recommended: C: Accept as a known limitation: a name moved away from a flagged instance can run beside the old work until Hassette restarts, as D6 already states.
findings.chosen: C: Accept as a known limitation: a name moved away from a flagged instance can run beside the old work until Hassette restarts, as D6 already states.

findings.title: Windows device names pass the instance-name check and become cache directories
findings.why_it_matters: Under D5 an instance name becomes a directory. `con`, `nul`, `aux`, `prn` and `com1` satisfy the instance-name pattern, and `unsafe_cache_path_reason` has no reserved-name check. On a native Windows host, cache creation for such an instance would misbehave. App keys have the same exposure today, so this is one more path to an existing gap.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: on a native Windows host, an instance named after a device such as `con` has an unusable default cache directory.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: on a native Windows host, an instance named after a device such as `con` has an unusable default cache directory.

findings.title: "Harmless" in D4 overlooks a stale click that stops a different healthy instance
findings.why_it_matters: D4 (what index an orphan reports) derives display order, so an index is resolved afresh per request. Suppose a page shows an orphan at index N, and then a config edit adds a configured instance that takes N. A stale click on the orphan's Stop now stops the new, healthy instance. D4's ratified sentence calls index shifts harmless. Today's position-keyed code has a similar stale-index risk, which restarts on reorder used to mask. The critic wants this named, and doesn't want a stored index or a null one. You stated that #3099 and #3100 ship in one release, so no release can show this. It exists only on `main` between the two merges.

findings.title: A running App's manifest goes stale on a reorder
findings.why_it_matters: An unrestarted instance keeps its old `AppManifest`. After a reorder-only edit, that object's `app_config` order disagrees with the registry's. Before this change, a position change restarted the instance, so the held object was always current. No code reads a live App's `app_manifest.app_config` by position today: the only `src` matches are lifecycle functions working from a manifest they were passed. Any future positional read on a live app would get another instance's config.
